1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it guards d4 and e5, prepares castling and keeps every set-up open. It also avoids the pin that 3.Nc3 allows, but it does not prepare e4, so White chooses a quieter, more patient game over a quick pawn centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Nimzo-Indian

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: The traditional move: the knight fights for e4 and d5 and prepares a broad pawn centre. The price is that Black can pin it with the bishop at once, so the game becomes a struggle over the centre rather than a quiet build-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of the king's bishop, which will press along the long diagonal against Black's queenside while White's king stays safe. White trades the quick e4 advance for lasting pressure, and Black can strike at the centre at once.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.name: Catalan Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.background: The Catalan is named after Catalonia: at the Barcelona tournament of 1929 the organisers asked Savielly Tartakower to create a new variation in homage to the region's chess history. It became part of the repertoire of leading players in the 1930s and 1940s, and Kramnik, Anand and Carlsen all used it in world championship games.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Qb3.strategy: Brings the queen out early to eye b7 and d5, but the bishop guards b7, so nothing is threatened. It leaves the d4 pawn without protection, and Black can develop with a gain of time against it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Qb3.name: Indian Defence

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.strategy: Pins the knight to the queen to disturb Black's usual development, but the pin is easily broken. Taking on f6 would let Black recapture with the queen, so no pawns are doubled; White gets an unusual set-up without a clear gain.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.name: Indian Defence: Seirawan Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.background: Also called the Neo-Indian Attack, it is named after the 1980s star Yasser Seirawan. It is rarely played, though the move order was already used by David Janowski against Edward Lasker in New York in 1922.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.strategy: A gambit: the pawn on g4 is undefended and the knight simply takes it. White hopes for a big pawn centre and open lines, but loosens its own kingside and has too little for the pawn once Black develops calmly.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.name: Indian Defence: Devin Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.background: Bill Devin played it in 1966 at the Lansing Chess Club, and by 1971 it was known in Michigan as the Devin Gambit. Grandmaster Shakhriyar Mamedyarov played it against Andrey Esipenko at the 2022 Tata Steel Masters.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a solid pawn pair on d5 and e6 and refuses to be pushed around. The cost is a light-squared bishop hemmed in by its own e-pawn; in return Black gets a sturdy position and aims for equality through patient manoeuvring.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will control e4 and d5 from a distance instead of occupying the centre with pawns. This stops White's e4 plan, frees the bishop from behind the e6 pawn and keeps Black flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and asks White what to do with the centre. Black accepts an unbalanced game: if White gains space by advancing the d-pawn, Black gets a queenside pawn majority and play against the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+.strategy: Develops with check and asks White how to block. Black is ready to exchange the bishop for the blocking piece or retreat it, content with a compact, solid game. White gets the space and the choice of structure, but Black has few weaknesses.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 to attack the c4 pawn and win queenside space. It develops nothing and does not address the centre, so White gets time to build a full centre at leisure.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 a6.name: Indian Defence: Dzindzi-Indian Defence

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.strategy: Takes the e4 square before White can occupy it with a pawn and pulls the knight toward the centre. It moves the same piece twice, though, and a developing move or the queen can hit the knight, so Black risks losing time.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.name: Indian Defence: Döry Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.background: Uncommon, but in 1937 it was the subject of a theme tournament in Vienna, won by Paul Keres.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5.strategy: The classical reply: Black takes a stand in the centre and waits for the bishop to show its hand. The d5 pawn blocks the long diagonal for now, but Black will have to decide later whether to hold the centre or take on c4 and give the pawn back.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, before the fianchettoed bishop has done any work. Black steers for an unbalanced structure with a queenside pawn majority, in which White's fianchetto set-up is not very dangerous.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7.strategy: A quiet developing move: Black prepares to castle, commits to nothing and waits to see White's set-up. The bishop declines both a pin and a central strike, leaving Black solid but a step behind in the fight for space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+.strategy: Makes White decide how to block: a knight allows a pin, while the bishop ends up on d2, where it does little. Black aims to trade off a minor piece for a solid game; the main lines are drawish, though some sidelines are sharper.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 e5.strategy: Throws the e-pawn forward at once, but White simply takes it, and after ...Ng4 attacks the pawn White can defend it. Black has given up a pawn for a little quick development, which is not enough.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 e5.name: Catalan Opening: Hungarian Gambit

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the knight to the king, so White cannot build the centre with e4 for now, and threatens to take on c3 and double White's pawns. Black commits to controlling e4 and to a lasting pawn weakness in return for the bishop pair, and keeps the central pawns flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre with a pawn and gives up the flexibility of the Indian set-ups for a solid, classical structure. The cost is the c8 bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6 pawn until Black finds a way to free it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, but without the pin White can push d5 and gain space, then build a broad centre. Black gets an unbalanced game with counterplay against that centre, but White holds the space and the easier development.
